column4: The section’s dictionary form عيلة names want; this verse places believers’ fear of عَيْلَةٍ beside God’s promise يُغْنِيكُمُ from His bounty. It turns the image of one person made sufficient into a communal fear of lost livelihood answered by divine provision.

The section’s dictionary gloss links عائل to poverty and أَغْنَى to making someone sufficient; here فقَرَاءَ are promised that Allah may يُغْنِهِم from His bounty. The same movement is applied to households formed by marriage.
The section glosses أَغْنَى as making another sufficient; this verse names God as the one who أَغْنَىٰ and أَقْنَىٰ, so sufficiency and the giving of possessions have an agent beyond the recipient.

The section’s dictionary account of خَيْر includes wealth, while Moses says he is فَقِيرٌ to whatever good God sends down. In context he has just watered the two women’s flock and withdrawn to the shade, so the verse makes need after useful labor and immediate shelter concrete.

The section defines richness as freedom from need; this verse reverses the scale by declaring people فقَرَاءُ إِلَى اللَّهِ and God الْغَنِيُّ الْحَمِيدُ. It makes material sufficiency one case within humanity’s deeper dependence.

The section explicitly contrasts its verb أَغْنَى—wealth received through another—with this person who is بَخِلَ and اسْتَغْنَىٰ, treating himself as self-sufficient. The contrast exposes the difference between being enriched and claiming independence.

The section contrasts divine enrichment with self-awarded sufficiency; here the human being’s seeing himself اسْتَغْنَىٰ leads to transgression. The verse marks self-sufficiency as a dangerous misreading of wealth.

The section’s dictionary note says a poor person may be called a سائل; this verse describes needy people whose restraint makes the uninformed count them as rich, and says they do not ask insistently. It prevents the reader from equating visible asking with the whole condition of poverty.

The section connects the poor person with the سائل at the door; this verse says that in the wealthy people’s أَمْوَالِهِمْ is a right لِلسَّائِلِ وَالْمَحْرُومِ. It makes the asker a claimant to wealth, not merely an interruption to its owner.

The section’s dictionary note calls the poor person a سائل; this verse pairs giving الْمَالَ with giving to the سَّائِلِينَ, alongside relatives, orphans, and the needy. It shows wealth moving toward the person who asks.

The section defines riches partly through possessions; this verse directs distribution so wealth will not be دُولَةً among the rich alone. It sets a boundary against the concentration that would leave the poor outside sufficiency.

The section follows poverty and enrichment as a change in condition; here a person whose Lord أَكْرَمَهُ وَنَعَّمَهُ concludes, “my Lord has honored me.” The neighboring 89:16 gives the inverse conclusion under restricted provision, and 89:17–20 correct the equation of wealth with honor.

The section traces want becoming sufficiency; here provision is قُدِرَ عَلَيْهِ and the person concludes, “my Lord has humiliated me.” The neighboring 89:15 supplies the opposite economic state, while 89:17–20 reject both status judgments as a measure of care for the poor.

The section says not to rebuke the سائل; this verse condemns failing to urge طَعَامِ الْمِسْكِينِ. It turns the response to need from mere restraint in speech toward active concern; 89:17 names the adjacent failure to honor the orphan.

The section’s dictionary gloss for عيل includes حرص, acquisitive greed; this verse says people love الْمَالَ حُبًّا جَمًّا. Its surrounding neglect of the poor makes that appetite a social harm, not just an inward feeling.

The section moves from want to sufficiency and places خير against the Hereafter; this verse says Allah expands and measures provision, then contrasts rejoicing in worldly life with its small share beside the Hereafter. It joins changing livelihood to the surah’s scale of what is truly better.

The section depicts poverty answered by enrichment; this verse states that the Lord expands الرِّزْقَ for whom He wills and measures it for whom He wills. It locates both abundance and constraint within the same act of provision.

The section identifies acquisitive greed as one trace of want; this verse says unrestricted expansion of provision would make people transgress, while God sends it down by measure. It explains why abundance is not simply multiplied without limit.

The section defines wealth as sufficiency; this verse tells the person of ample means to spend from that means and the one whose provision is restricted from what God gave him, then promises ease after hardship. It measures obligation to actual provision rather than imagined abundance.
The section glosses أَغْنَى as making someone sufficient; this verse says that whoever relies on Allah finds that He is حَسْبُهُ, and joins that sufficiency to provision from an unexpected source.

The section’s dictionary account of نعمة points to ease and good living; this verse describes abundant provision arriving from every place, followed by the taste of hunger and fear when the people deny God’s blessings. It stages comfort and deprivation as opposite conditions.
The section names malnutrition as poverty’s bodily trace; this verse says the Lord fed Quraysh مِن جُوعٍ and secured them from fear. It gives bodily hunger a direct counterpart in divine provision.

The section’s dictionary gloss for خَيْر includes wealth, and its gloss for عيل includes acquisitive حرص; this verse joins الْخَيْرِ to intense love. In context it names the human pull toward wealth that the section’s greed gloss diagnoses.

The section’s dictionary gloss for خَيْر identifies it as property; this verse uses تَرَكَ خَيْرًا for what a person leaves behind and directs a bequest from it. The legal context confirms the word’s material sense.

The section’s dictionary says wealth is called خَيْر only when it is abundant and from a good source; this verse states that bad and good are not equal even if كَثْرَةُ الْخَبِيثِ impresses you. It marks abundance alone as no proof of good or clean wealth.

The section commands that the asker not be rebuked; this verse describes spending wealth without following it with reminder or injury. It connects giving material support to preserving the recipient’s dignity.

The section says not to drive away the سائل; this verse says a known kind word and pardon are better than charity followed by harm. It sets the dignity of the petitioner above the giver’s display of payment.

The section’s instruction not to rebuke the asker has a direct boundary here: charity is nullified by reminders and injury. The verse shows how a gift can fail to relieve need when the giver humiliates its recipient.

The section connects enrichment with wealth and the poor petitioner; this verse says the faithful have a known right in their wealth. Neighboring 70:25 identifies its recipients as the asker and the deprived, completing the claim.

The section’s dictionary note calls the poor person a سائل; this verse names لِلسَّائِلِ وَالْمَحْرُومِ as recipients of the known right in wealth. Neighboring 70:24 supplies the claim that this right is held within their wealth.

The section describes need answered by enrichment from فضل; this verse says Satan يَعِدُكُمُ الْفَقْرَ while God promises forgiveness and bounty. It names fear of poverty as a pressure that can turn a person away from giving.

The section closes by telling the recipient of نعمة to speak of it; this verse joins gratitude for God’s favor with the promise of increase. It frames received sufficiency as a gift to acknowledge rather than a self-made status.

The section places need and blessing together; this verse says every نعمة people have is from Allah, then says they cry to Him when harm touches them. It links received good living to the same dependence exposed by hardship.

The section’s dictionary gloss for نعمة describes comfort and good living; this verse says people will be asked about النَّعِيمِ. It adds accountability to the comfort whose arrival the section calls a blessing.

The section defines richness partly as having few needs and many possessions; when asked what to spend, this verse answers الْعَفْوَ, the surplus. It makes the boundary between sufficiency and excess a basis for giving.

The section’s dictionary gloss for خَيْر can mean wealth; this verse calls wealth and children adornment of worldly life, then says the enduring good deeds are better. It distinguishes material “good” from what remains with God.

The section depicts the poor petitioner at someone’s door and forbids harshness; this verse says that when relatives, orphans, and needy people are present at an inheritance division, they should be given something and addressed graciously. It supplies a concrete setting for receiving need with generosity.

The section’s dictionary form سائل means a poor petitioner; this verse says provision on earth is سَوَاءً لِّلسَّائِلِينَ. If سائلين here means those who ask or seek provision, it extends the link from a petitioner at a door to provision made available to seekers; that lexical bridge is uncertain.

The section moves from receiving sufficiency to encountering a poor person; this verse describes feeding the مسكين, orphan, and captive despite love for the food. It makes a response to need an act of giving from what one values.

The section names poor nutrition as a bodily trace of want; this verse pictures feeding during a day ذِي مَسْغَبَةٍ, severe hunger. Neighboring 90:15–16 specify the vulnerable people reached by that response.

The section’s image concerns a person’s need and the response to someone arriving for help; this verse identifies a near orphan as one recipient in the passage’s feeding response. Neighboring 90:14 supplies the day of hunger and 90:16 names the needy person in misery.

The section says the poor person may be a سائل; this verse names a مِسْكِينًا ذَا مَتْرَبَةٍ, a needy person in misery, as the next recipient in the feeding passage. Neighboring 90:14 supplies the hunger setting and 90:15 the orphan.

The section’s whole-surah context pairs the former orphan’s care with restraint toward the asker; this verse condemns forcefully driving away the orphan. It shows the opposite treatment of a vulnerable person once need is no longer one’s own.
The section says not to rebuke the سائل; this verse condemns failing to urge food for the مسكين. It makes disregard for the poor a boundary against the section’s dignified response to need.

The section’s dictionary gloss for عيل uses حرص for acquisitive greed; this verse uses أَحْرَصَ for people’s desire to live, even wishing for a thousand years. The changed object of desire cautions against reducing the source’s greed gloss to one wording or object.

The section’s dictionary gloss links عيل to حرص in the sense of acquisition; this verse calls the Messenger حَرِيصٌ عَلَيْكُم, concerned for you, then describes his compassion. It marks a distinct, benevolent sense of the wording rather than acquisitive greed.
The section glosses أَغْنَى as making someone sufficient; this verse asks whether Allah is not كَافٍ عَبْدَهُ. It states sufficiency through God’s care rather than through possessions.

The section includes fear of want answered by divine enrichment; this verse forbids killing children مِّنْ إِمْلَاقٍ and answers that God provides for parents and children. It makes feared poverty within a household a direct case of provision coming from beyond the household.

The section names fear of poverty in 9:28 and God’s enrichment from bounty; here the fear is that children will bring إِمْلَاقًا, and God says He provides for them and their parents. It applies the same fear-and-provision relation to future need.

The section traces poverty becoming wealth and asks the reader to see the giver behind it; this verse says God has favored some over others in provision, then depicts those favored withholding it from those under their authority. It makes unequal provision and refusal to share visible.

The section connects the poor person to the asker and to wealth; this verse names the poor and needy among the recipients of alms. It specifies a communal route by which wealth reaches people in want.

The section develops the poor person as someone who asks and the enriched person’s encounter with him; this verse answers a question about spending by directing it to parents, relatives, orphans, the needy, and travelers. It maps giving onto concrete relations and recipients.

The section’s petitioner is someone in need; this verse commands giving the relative, needy person, and traveler their due. It turns the encounter with need into an allotted right, and its warning against waste sets a limit on the giver’s use of wealth.

The section depicts a poor petitioner meeting someone who has been enriched; this verse commands giving relatives, the needy, and the traveler their due, and connects that act with seeking God’s face. It is another direct formulation of wealth moving toward need.

The section shows that need can be concealed: restrained poor people may be mistaken for rich. This verse says that concealing charity while giving it to the poor is better, a specific way of meeting need without making the recipient’s exposure the point.

The section defines richness partly through having little need, and identifies acquisitive greed as a trace of want; this verse warns against both a closed hand and spending everything, which leaves a person blamed and destitute. It gives the image a boundary of measured use.

The section contrasts want, sufficiency, and acquisitive greed; this verse describes the faithful as neither extravagant nor miserly, but balanced between them. It makes sufficiency a measured relation to wealth rather than its maximum accumulation.

The section describes want’s spiritual trace as acquisitive greed; this verse says the human being was created impatient or anxious. Neighboring 70:20–21 specify the responses to harm and good that make this disposition relevant to poverty and provision.

The section traces want into an inward condition; this verse says that when evil touches a person he becomes anxious. Neighboring 70:21 supplies the opposite response when good reaches him—he withholds—completing a specific need-and-abundance pattern.

The section’s dictionary gloss links poverty with acquisitive greed; this verse says that when good touches the person, he withholds. Neighboring 70:20 gives his anxiety under harm, making the two verses a direct reversal between deprivation and received good.

The section says enrichment comes through another’s hand, not a self-awarded status; this verse condemns people who withhold what Allah gave them from His bounty while thinking it good for them. It directly opposes receiving wealth and then treating it as grounds to keep it from others.

The section ends with the blessing to be spoken of; this verse condemns miserliness and concealing what God gave from His bounty. It gives concealment of received provision as the opposite response to recognizing a blessing.

The section describes wealth and acquisitive greed; this verse condemns hoarding gold and silver without spending in God’s way. Neighboring 9:35 gives the consequence of that hoarding, while this ayah identifies the withholding itself.

The section describes wealth as a provision that can free another from need; this verse says the hoarded gold and silver are heated and used to mark their owners. Neighboring 9:34 identifies the hoarding, and this ayah reverses retained wealth into bodily punishment.

The section identifies acquisitive greed as an inward trace of want; this verse says that even if people held the treasuries of their Lord’s mercy, they would withhold them for fear of spending, and that humanity is miserly. It gives a direct counterpoint to sufficiency received and passed on.

The section’s ayah 93:4 says the Hereafter is better than the first life, while its dictionary discussion turns to material wealth; this verse depicts rivalry in wealth and children as part of worldly life and contrasts it with the Hereafter. It makes material abundance part of a passing order.

The section portrays sufficiency as something provided by another; this verse depicts wealth spent in God’s way as a seed multiplied many times over. It gives a concrete image of provision not being diminished by giving.

The section glosses enrichment as making someone sufficient; this verse says that what people spend, God replaces, and names Him the best of providers. It directly joins expenditure to provision returned by the giver.

The section shows the poor man as someone unable to meet his needs; this verse pictures creatures that do not carry their provision and says Allah provides for them and for people. It places sufficiency in provision received rather than in the creature’s stockpiling.

The section names acquisition greed as a trace of want; this verse says righteousness is not attained until one spends from what one loves. It marks the inward attachment to wealth and the action that loosens it.
